title: The Tyrant in Sheol, Assyria Broken, Philistia Warned
summary: God promises compassion for Jacob, return to the land, and rest from forced labor, and he gives his people a taunt song over the fallen king of Babylon. The tyrant who wanted to climb above the stars of God is brought down to Sheol, where the dead kings greet him with scorn, and he is denied even a proper grave. The chapter closes with God's oath to break Assyria on his own mountain and an oracle warning the Philistines not to celebrate too soon.
story: Chapter 13 announced Babylon's overthrow. Chapter 14 tells what that overthrow will mean for God's people: return, rest, and a song. Babylon, the power that would one day carry Judah into exile, is pictured as already fallen and mocked. Then the focus shifts to Assyria, the empire actually pressing on Judah in Isaiah's lifetime, with a sworn promise that its yoke will be broken. Finally a dated oracle turns to Philistia, Judah's neighbor on the coast. The chapter thus runs from the far future (Babylon), to the near future (Assyria), to the present moment (the year Ahaz died), and insists that the same purpose of God stands over all three.
historical:
The king of Babylon in verse 4 is not named, and scholars have proposed several candidates. Some think of the Assyrian king Sargon II, who also ruled Babylon and who died in battle in 705 BC, his body apparently never recovered for burial, which would fit the unburied tyrant of verses 18 to 20. Others think of Sennacherib, of Nebuchadnezzar, or of Nabonidus, the last Neo-Babylonian king. Many read the poem as intentionally typical, a portrait of the imperial tyrant as such, which the book applies to the king of Babylon because Babylon came to stand for the empire that exiled Judah.

Verses 24 to 27 return to Assyria, which dominated Judah throughout Isaiah's ministry. The promise to break Assyria “in My land” and “on My mountain” fits the events of 701 BC, when Sennacherib's army besieged Jerusalem and withdrew (Isaiah 36 and 37). The oracle to Philistia is dated to the year King Ahaz died, which is itself disputed: about 727 BC on one reckoning, about 715 BC on another. The broken rod that had struck Philistia may be an Assyrian king who had recently died, such as Tiglath-pileser III (died 727 BC), whose campaigns had crushed the Philistine cities; some take it as Ahaz or another ruler. The Philistines, who held the coastal cities of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath, repeatedly rebelled against Assyria and sought allies, and verse 32 pictures their envoys in Jerusalem looking for Judah's support.
cultural:
Sheol (verses 9, 11, and 15) was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a shadowy place beneath the earth where all the dead went, great and small. Its inhabitants are called rephaim, shades or ghosts, weak and without their former power. The poem imagines the dead kings rising from their thrones in Sheol to greet the newcomer with mockery: he is now as weak as they are. Proper burial in a family or royal tomb mattered enormously in the ancient world; to be left unburied, or cast out of one's grave, was a final disgrace. That is the fate of the tyrant in verses 18 to 20.

The language of verses 12 to 14 draws on the religious imagery of Israel's neighbors. The day star, son of the dawn (Hebrew Helel ben Shachar), is most likely the morning star, the planet Venus, which rises brilliantly before sunrise and then fades as the sun climbs. Texts from ancient Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, describe the gods meeting on Mount Zaphon in the far north, and Baal's palace there; the mount of assembly “in the far reaches of the north” echoes that picture. Ugaritic myth also tells of a god, Athtar, who tries to sit on Baal's throne and proves too small for it. Isaiah uses this familiar imagery to mock a human king who aimed to make himself divine.
literary: The heart of the chapter is a taunt song (verse 4, Hebrew mashal) in the rhythm often used for funeral laments, with a longer line followed by a shorter one. Its opening word, How, is the typical first word of a lament (compare Lamentations 1:1), turned into mockery. The poem moves in scenes: the earth at rest and the cedars of Lebanon rejoicing (verses 4 to 8), the dead kings greeting the tyrant in Sheol (verses 9 to 11), the boast of the day star and his fall (verses 12 to 15), and onlookers staring at his unburied corpse (verses 16 to 21). The movement is up and down: I will ascend, I will raise my throne, I will make myself like the Most High, and then, but you will be brought down. Verses 24 to 27 use the words plan and purpose several times to set God's counsel against the counsel of kings.

outline.t: Compassion for Jacob and return to the land
The taunt over the king of Babylon: the earth rejoices and Sheol greets him
The day star who tried to climb above God is brought down
The unburied tyrant and the sweeping away of Babylon
God's oath to break Assyria on his mountain
An oracle to Philistia in the year Ahaz died

doctrines.note: The tyrant's sin is the oldest one: the desire to be like the Most High. Pride that refuses creaturely limits ends in the Pit, the lowest place.
God's plan for the whole earth stands, and his outstretched hand cannot be turned back. The rise and fall of empires belongs to his purpose.
Death levels every ruler. The powerful who oppressed the nations become weak like everyone else in Sheol, and God's justice reaches the tyrant even there.
Behind the promise of return stands God's covenant choice of Jacob, renewed as he will once again choose Israel. The chapter also opens a door for the foreigner to join the house of Jacob.

words.note: Helel, the day star or shining one, used only here in the Hebrew Bible. It likely names the morning star. Jerome's Latin translation rendered it lucifer, meaning light-bearer, the ordinary Latin name for the morning star, and from that rendering came the later use of Lucifer as a name for Satan.

Sheol, the realm of the dead. In the Old Testament it is the place where all the dead go, not specifically a place of punishment, though the lowest depths of the Pit (verse 15) carry a sense of disgrace. Here Sheol is personified as eager to greet the tyrant.
Mashal, a proverb, saying, or taunt. The word covers wise sayings (it names the book of Proverbs) as well as mocking songs. In verse 4 it introduces a satirical lament over a fallen king.

Yaats, to counsel, plan, or purpose. It appears three times in verses 24 to 27. Kings made plans for conquest, but the chapter insists that what the LORD of Hosts has purposed will stand, and no one can thwart it.

christ: Jesus drew on this chapter when he warned Capernaum that, though it would be lifted up to heaven, it would be brought down to Hades (Luke 10:15), applying the fall of the proud tyrant to a town that had seen his works and did not repent. The deeper link is a contrast. The tyrant grasped at equality with the Most High and was cast down. Paul describes Christ, who was in very nature God, as refusing to grasp at that equality and instead humbling himself to death on a cross, after which God exalted him (Philippians 2:6-11). The New Testament also presents the fall of the dark powers through Christ's victory (Luke 10:18), which is one reason Christian tradition came to read these verses of Satan, though Isaiah's first subject is a human king.

hard.q: Is Isaiah 14:12 about the fall of Satan?
hard.a: The text itself says it is a taunt against the king of Babylon (verse 4), and verse 16 calls him a man. Most modern interpreters, including many conservative ones, therefore read verses 12 to 15 primarily as a portrait of a human tyrant, described with images from the religious myths of the day. From the early centuries of the church, however, many Christian writers read the passage as also describing the fall of Satan, whose pride they saw as the pattern behind every proud ruler, and the Latin rendering lucifer attached that name to him. Some readers today hold a double reference: the human king is the subject, but his boast mirrors a spiritual rebellion behind him, as Ezekiel 28 describes the king of Tyre in similar terms. Others think this reading goes beyond what the text supports. Either way, the passage does not give a detailed account of Satan's origin, and its main point, that pride which reaches for God's throne ends in the Pit, stands on every reading.

questions: The tyrant's boast is five times I will. Where do you see that same desire to make yourself like the Most High, in public life or in your own heart?
The dead kings tell the tyrant, you have become like us. What does the certainty of death do to human claims of power?
The Philistine envoys are told that the LORD has founded Zion as a refuge for his afflicted people. What are you tempted to trust for security instead?
